title: Leading KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit
web_title: 5. Leading KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit
book_title: Chapter 5: Management on Trial — Leading KPIs & Walking the Talk
question: Do PCBL's leading operating indicators and management's record of keeping promises support the claim that carbon black plus specialty chemicals can compound, or do they say the cycle and the balance sheet are in charge?

epigraph.quote: “Over the next 30 months, the cash flows from the two combined businesses would be more than enough to pay this entire money.”
epigraph.author: Dr Sanjiv Goenka, Chairman, PCBL, call on the Aquapharm acquisition, 28 November 2023

web_blocks.html: Reported profit tells you what happened last quarter; leading indicators tell you what the next four quarters will probably show. For PCBL, six measures lead the financials: carbon black volume and mix, EBITDA per tonne, plant utilisation, power sales, Aquapharm's quarterly EBITDA, and working capital with gearing. The second half of this chapter lines up what management promised on its calls since May 2023 against what the numbers later showed. It scores each promise as delivered, partly delivered, missed or unproven, and gives a single KPI health judgement. Management's EBITDA figures include other income, so they run slightly above the feed's operating profit; Chapter 6 reconciles the two [18][4].

web_blocks.takeaway: Three KPIs are healthy or watchable (volume mix, power, EBITDA per tonne), and three are weak (utilisation, Aquapharm, gearing). The pattern is a core carbon black business recovering inside a group whose acquisition and balance sheet are not.

web_blocks.title: KPI 1: carbon black volume and mix

web_blocks.caption: Carbon black volume and mix, FY23 to H1 FY27
web_blocks.takeaway: Volume grew 19.5% and 12.1% in the two years after the Chennai plant opened, then slowed to 3.8% and turned negative in H1 FY27. Shares are computed from published tonnages (my calc); performance (non-tyre industrial rubber) grades, not specialty, took most of the mix shift from FY23 to FY26.

web_blocks.html: The H1 FY27 decline is a decision, not a demand collapse. In Q2 FY27 volume fell 17.0% to 134,180 t. The CFO called it “primarily a margin decision”, letting go of South-East Asian and domestic spot orders that did not earn a contribution [40]. Exports dropped from 38.4% of Q2 volume a year earlier to 30.8% (my calc). The arithmetic of the guide is awkward. A 7% rise on FY2026 means 662,283 t for FY2027, so H2 would need 374,589 t. That is 23.6% above H2 FY2026's 303,135 t and above any quarter in the last two years (my calc). The MD called the 7% guide “a little bit challenging right now” on 2 November 2026 [40]. We read volume as healthy in mix, weak in absolute terms, and under management's control.

web_blocks.title: KPI 2: carbon black EBITDA per tonne

web_blocks.caption: EBITDA per tonne against the ₹1,000-a-year path promised in February 2023
rows: about ₹21,450; about ₹20,400 net of the Q2 refund
web_blocks.takeaway: The CFO's February 2023 promise of about ₹1,000 a year of EBITDA per tonne was beaten for three years and reversed by about ₹4,000 in the fourth. H1 FY27 is back above the path only after counting a tariff refund and inventory gains.

web_blocks.caption: Recent quarters: what moved EBITDA per tonne
rows: Spread already narrowing before the FY26 slide [9]
Formula lag in a falling crude market; derived from the H1 figure [34]
Falling crude, 50% US tariff, export volume −13% [35]
Implied by the FY26 total of ₹14,939 (my calc); “not much improvement at EBITDA per ton level” [36]
About ₹70 Cr of low-cost inventory gain, or about ₹4,560 per tonne (my calc) [38]

web_blocks.takeaway: Quarter to quarter the figure swung between ₹13,800 and ₹22,900 on crude, inventory and a refund while the plants and contracts did not change. Removing the Q1 inventory gain and the Q2 refund leaves an underlying H1 FY27 of about ₹17,900 per tonne (my calc), above the FY26 level but below FY25.

web_blocks.html: Management reiterated on 2 November 2026 “double-digit growth in average EBITDA per tonne over FY26 levels”, which is at least ₹16,433. It has also cited 14–15%, or ₹17,030–₹17,180 (my calc) [40][38]. Our underlying H1 figure of about ₹17,900 sits above that, so the guidance looks achievable even if the H2 inventory gain reverses. The longer promise is harder: the CFO said on 3 February 2026 that “we should be reaching somewhere near Rs. 24,000-25,000/ton in next five years” [35], which is 60–67% above FY26 and above the FY24 peak of ₹20,018. Chapter 4 explains why a feedstock-led spread cannot be treated as a moat.

web_blocks.caption: Carbon black utilisation on year-end nameplate
rows: Capacity label “2023” in the company chart [19][24]
90 KTPA added in Jan and Mar 2026 [14][3]
Capacity raised from 130 KTPA during FY26 [36][14]
web_blocks.takeaway: PCBL added 214 KTPA between FY23 and FY26 while volume rose 174 kt, so utilisation never exceeded FY25's 75.5%. Nameplate overstates real capacity. Management said Chennai's gross 147,000 t would yield only 120,000–125,000 t, so true utilisation is somewhat higher than shown [24].

web_blocks.caption: Co-generation: generation, external sales and realisation
web_blocks.takeaway: The roughly 60% of generation sold has been constant, so realisation drives the upside. Q2 FY27's ₹5.34 against ₹3.76 a year earlier was worth about ₹17 Cr in the quarter. The 12 MW Tamil Nadu unit promised for FY26 is still “CoD FY27”, so installed capacity has stayed at 122 MW [24][6][9][14][16][18][3].

web_blocks.caption: Aquapharm quarterly revenue, EBITDA and volume against the ₹75 Cr goal
web_blocks.takeaway: Against the figures published at signing, FY26 revenue is 28% lower and EBITDA 61% lower. Revenue is flat at about ₹1,420–1,443 Cr for two years while the margin slid from 13.7% to 9.7% in the latest quarter. Q2 FY25 is omitted because the sources conflict. [6][10][12][18][14][77]

web_blocks.html: Aquapharm's volume fell 1.4% in FY2026 and 6.9% in H1 FY27 (47,238 t against 50,744 t). H1 EBITDA was ₹89 Cr against ₹98 Cr, down 9.2% on revenue up 6.4% (my calc) [18][14]. Oil and gas volume fell 19.5% in FY26. Management attributes the weakness to yellow phosphorus and other input spikes, US oil and gas destocking, and Chinese competition [14][36]. Aquapharm's chief executive, Rohit Narang, said on 2 November 2026 that anti-dumping on HEDP and ATMP is “provisional right now”. He added that no impact is in the forecast [40]. Against the ₹3,850 Cr consideration, FY26 EBITDA of ₹162 Cr is a 4.2% yield (4.3% on the ₹3,800 Cr headline enterprise value; my calc). The audited segment note shows Chemicals PBIT of only ₹17.43 Cr on ₹4,226 Cr of segment assets [3].

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital days, borrowings and coverage
web_blocks.takeaway: Working capital improved sharply in FY26 (debtor days 78 to 62, CCC 57 to 35), but half of the improvement was a crude-price effect that has reversed. By September inventories were up 93% and payables up 68% since March. Net debt of 4.2x company EBITDA in FY26 (₹4,536 Cr over ₹1,081 Cr, including other income) is above the 2x ceiling the CFO set in October 2024. Chapter 6 covers coverage and the leverage ladder. [4][14][18][36]

web_blocks.takeaway: Capacity plans are sound in size but late in time. Every new-material milestone has moved right, and the only route to 1 Mt depends on a clearance not yet received. FY30 EBITDA of ₹4,000 Cr needs more than a tripling, so we treat it as an aspiration rather than a base case.

web_blocks.html: The addressable market for the core product is growing slowly, not fast. India's domestic demand grows at 3.7% a year, with tyres, almost 80% of demand, growing at 3.3% [3]. PCBL's FY2025 domestic volume of 351,762 t is about 30% of the 1.17 Mt demand (my calc). Domestic growth must therefore come from share, from specialty (7.6% a year) or from export. Management sees Europe as the opening. Western Europe imports about 500,000 t a year, once about 80% from Russia, and India supplies close to 100,000 t [36]. That is a credible runway, and the runway is for volume that earns a spread, not for an expanding moat.

Each row below lists the promise verbatim, who made it and on which call, what happened, and our score. We condensed 34 audited promises into the 18 most decision-relevant rows; where rows combine two promises, both received the same score. The tally for all 34 follows the table.

web_blocks.caption: Scorecard for all 34 audited promises, by theme
web_blocks.takeaway: Only 4 of 34 promises (12%) were fully met and 10 (29%) were missed outright. Aquapharm has no delivered promise out of 8.

web_blocks.html: An honest scorecard separates the kinds of promise. When the question was whether a plant would be built and ramped, management largely delivered. The Chennai greenfield and brownfield lines are running and volume rose 39% in three years to 618,956 t [14]. When the question was whether a new business would deliver a number, or the balance sheet would be repaired, the record is poor. Three of the ten missed items are timing misses of 12–22 months (Tamil Nadu phase 1 and the nano-silicon plant and pilot). The other seven are financial promises that were wrong in size, such as the ₹525 Cr Aquapharm EBITDA for FY26 against the ₹162 Cr delivered. Management has acknowledged some of this: “FY '25 was a bit challenging year for Aquapharm” (MD, 29 Apr 2025) and “while Aquapharm has not grown as we anticipated” (CFO, 3 Feb 2026) [32][35]. Our judgement is that the carbon black team is a competent operator and that the group's capital allocation record on acquisitions and debt is weak. Leadership turnover compounds the problem. The MD resigned on 3 November 2025, seventeen days after leading the Q2 FY26 call. Aquapharm's CEO resigned in February 2026 and was replaced in May 2026 after an interim period [3][35][82].

web_blocks.title: KPI health: PASS_WITH_WATCH
paragraphs: We rate KPI health PASS_WITH_WATCH, at the weak end of that band. In favour: record FY2026 volume of 618,956 t, a specialty share that rose from 9.1% to 12.6% and power realisation up 42%. EBITDA per tonne is back above the FY26 level on an underlying ₹17,900, debtor days are down from 97 to 62, and the carbon black plants ramped on time or slightly late. Against: utilisation of 63.9% on nameplate, Aquapharm EBITDA at 56% of the ₹75 Cr goal and volume down 8.9% in H1 FY27. Net debt is 3.95x LTM company EBITDA (total debt 4.15x, CARE's trigger basis) with FY26 interest cover of 2.5x, and the delivered-or-partly record is only 14 of 34 promises [4][14][18].

We would not rate it a pass because two KPIs (Aquapharm and gearing) are failing and two more depend on crude. We would not rate it a fail, because the core carbon black earnings engine produced ₹925 Cr of EBITDA in FY26 and about ₹617 Cr in H1 FY27. Management's controllable promises were also largely kept. The business is a recovering cyclical with a weak acquisition inside it, not a business whose indicators are broken.

web_blocks.html: What would change our mind. We would move to FAIL on either of two triggers. The first is H2 FY2027 carbon black EBITDA per tonne, net of inventory and refund effects, falling below ₹16,500 while volume stays below 140,000 t a quarter. The second is Aquapharm quarterly EBITDA staying under ₹45 Cr through Q4 FY27 with total debt still above 4 times LTM company EBITDA at March 2027 (4.15x at September 2026, CARE's own trigger basis). We would move to PASS if utilisation passes 75% with underlying EBITDA per tonne at or above ₹17,000. Aquapharm would also need to reach ₹60 Cr a quarter, and net debt to company EBITDA to fall below 3x.

For an owner, the KPIs say the carbon black engine works and the acquisition has not yet earned its place. Chapter 6 follows the cash. It asks how much of the recovery shows up in free cash flow, how heavy the debt really is, and whether the earnings are of good quality.

book_paragraphs: Charlie Munger liked to say, “Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome.” I want you to hold that sentence in mind as we do something uncomfortable in this chapter: we audit the people running PCBL against their own words. Before that, though, let us look at the six gauges on the dashboard, because gauges lead and accounts follow. Picture a control room with six dials: how many tonnes the furnaces made, how much money each tonne earned, how full the plants are, how much power was sold, what Aquapharm earns each quarter, and how much working capital and debt the group carries. Four dials are amber, one is green, and one, Aquapharm, is red.

Start with volume. Carbon black volume rose from 445,184 tonnes in FY23 to 618,956 tonnes in FY26, an 11.6% compound rate, almost exactly what the CFO promised on 17 October 2023 when he said, “we believe that next five to six years we can grow at lower double digit, may be 12% to 13% kind of growth.” But look at the last two columns of my table. FY26 growth was only 3.8% and the first half of FY27 fell 8.9%. In Q2 FY27 the volume dropped 17% to 134,180 tonnes. Is that demand collapsing? No. The CFO told investors on 2 November 2026 that “we are not chasing volumes. We would rather keep this capacity spare.” They walked away from low-margin orders in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Vietnam and Thailand and from domestic spot sales.

Now do the arithmetic the management guide invites. A 7% rise over FY26 means 662,283 tonnes. Half the year is gone and 287,694 tonnes are in the bag, so the second half needs 374,589 tonnes, which is 23.6% more than the second half of last year. When an analyst probed this, the Managing Director said the 7% guide was “a little bit challenging right now.” I appreciate the candour, and I would plan on flat-to-lower volumes for FY27.

The second dial is the one that matters most: what each tonne earns. In February 2023 the CFO told analysts, “we took 2022 as base… in next four, five years on an average every year there should be about a Rs.1000 kind of increase in our EBITDA performance.” Walk through what followed. From about ₹15,000 a tonne the figure rose to ₹17,405, ₹20,018 and ₹19,930 for three years, ahead of the promised path every year. Then FY26 brought ₹14,939, about ₹4,000 below where the promise implied it should be. H1 FY27 looks magnificent at about ₹21,450, but I would not frame that number. About ₹70 crore of it was cheap feedstock sold at higher prices, worth about ₹4,560 a tonne in Q1, and ₹2,300 a tonne in Q2 was a refund of American tariffs. Strip both and you get about ₹17,900, which is still better than FY26 and still inside what management guided. Notice what the CFO said on 30 April 2026 when asked about a jump in profit: “There's not much improvement at EBITDA per ton level. So, the real impact of all the initiatives… is yet to come.” That is the voice of a man who does not oversell, and I give him credit for it.

Then there is utilisation. PCBL added 214,000 tonnes of capacity between FY23 and FY26 and volume rose by only 174,000 tonnes, so the plants have never run fuller than the 75.5% they reached in FY25. Today, annualised H1 volume is 63.9% of the 900,000 tonnes on the nameplate. Fixed costs do not care about the reasons. When plants run at two-thirds, every extra tonne sold falls mostly to profit, which is the good news for volume recovery, and every missing tonne costs a full share of fixed cost, which is the bad news now. Power, the fourth dial, is the cheerful exception. The tail gas of the furnaces drives 122 megawatts, about 60% of the electricity is sold, and the price rose from ₹3.76 to ₹5.34 a unit between Q2 FY26 and Q2 FY27, adding about ₹17 crore in that quarter alone.

Now the red dial. On 28 November 2023 the Chairman told investors that Aquapharm's forecast EBITDA was “380, 430, 525” for FY24, FY25 and FY26 and that its revenue was “INR 2,045 crores” with a 20% margin. What actually arrived? ₹194 crore in FY25, which is 45% of the 430 promised, and ₹162 crore in FY26, which is 31% of the 525. The margin fell from 20% to 11.2%, and in Q2 FY27 it was 9.7%. The Aquapharm CEO at the time, Suresh Kalra, said on 17 October 2025 that quarterly EBITDA of ₹75 crore “by this year end, that is right. So, that is where our exit is planned.” The next two quarters delivered ₹35 crore and ₹29 crore. His successor, Rohit Narang, has since said anti-dumping duty on HEDP and ATMP is “provisional right now.” You and I should weigh that: a ₹3,800 crore purchase now yields ₹162 crore of EBITDA, about 4.3% a year before tax, interest or capital to keep the plants running.

That leads straight to the promise that matters most to a lender. On the call of 28 November 2023 the Chairman said, “Over the next 30 months, the cash flows from the two combined businesses would be more than enough to pay this entire money.” Thirty months later is roughly May 2026. At 31 March 2026 net borrowings were ₹4,536 crore. The CFO had said on 30 October 2024, “we are not comfortable with our debt to EBITDA beyond 2”; net debt was 3.6 times company EBITDA at the end of FY25 and 4.2 times at the end of FY26. On 12 August 2024 he described five-year cash flow of “almost INR9800-10,000 crores”, enough “to also repay the entire debt”; two years in, cash from operations totals ₹2,336 crore, about 58% of the straight-line pace. I do not think anyone lied. I think forecasts made at a cyclical high turned out to be a poor guide to a trough year.

The sixth dial, working capital and gearing, flatters in the annual numbers and warns in the half-year, so let us look at it slowly. In FY26 debtor days fell from 78 to 62 and the cash conversion cycle from 57 to 35 days, and a working-capital release of ₹529 crore helped net borrowings fall by ₹454 crore. The CFO said on 3 February 2026 that this came from better terms with customers and vendors, better inventory management and the fact that “crude came down in this period”. Then crude went from about $60 at the start of 2026 to about $110 by November, and by 30 September inventories had risen from ₹1,024 crore to ₹1,981 crore while trade payables rose from ₹1,447 crore to ₹2,428 crore. Net trade working capital rose only ₹170 crore, which is why gross debt rose just ₹102 crore. But read what that means: supplier credit funded nearly the whole build, and the FY26 release was largely a crude-price round trip, not a permanent improvement in how the business runs.

So how should you score it? I count 34 promises in the audit table. Four were delivered in full: the FY24 volume milestone, the specialty additions, and the two promises about the Chennai ramp. Ten were met in part, ten were missed, and ten cannot yet be judged. Of the eight Aquapharm promises, none was delivered; five were missed. Of the fourteen about carbon black plants and operations, ten were delivered or partly delivered. The pattern is as clear as I have seen in a flagship company: management delivers what its engineers can build and misses what depends on a new market, on an acquired business or on crude. The nano-silicon plant is the sharpest example. In January 2025 the CFO said the pilot would be commissioned “in the next few months' time”. It started creating samples on 2 November 2026, 22 months later, and the commercial plant moved from “Phase 1 by FY27” in September 2025 to “end of FY'28” by February 2026.

Now the runway. Management's Vision 2030 asks for revenue of ₹16,000 crore, EBITDA of about ₹4,000 crore, specialty at 45% of revenue and net debt below one times EBITDA. From FY26's ₹1,081 crore that needs 38.7% compound growth for four years. I looked for where the growth comes from, and about ₹1,400 crore of the ₹2,600 crore increment sits in conductive and battery products that have not yet made a commercial sale. The CFO told investors on 30 April 2026, “from 2030 perspective, we are very confident, we remain on track.” I treat that as an ambition rather than a forecast. The nearer runway is more modest and more believable: Indian demand growing 3.7% a year, Europe, specialty at 7.6% a year, and 100,000 tonnes of Andhra capacity that, on management's own sequence of clearance and construction, arrives in FY29 or FY30 and not by the March 2028 date given in April 2025.

It is worth noticing how often the sceptics were right in advance. On 30 October 2024 an analyst said, “you were guiding earlier around 15-20% volume growth. In this quarter sir we had witnessed only, you can say, flattish volumes only,” and Aquapharm's FY25 volume came in at 95,806 tonnes. On 23 July 2025 another asked about “diluting the overall ROCE”, and the CFO answered that the internal expectation was “at least 17-18% kind of minimum return on invested capital, but it takes time to reach to those numbers. In 3-4 years' time.” Group ROCE in FY26 was 8%, and the Chemicals segment earned 0.4% before tax on its assets. On 2 November 2026 an analyst asked how much of the ₹200–250 crore cost programme was structural, and the CFO said, “It is not much at this stage.” I give management credit for the straight answer and the sceptics credit for asking the right question a year early. As an owner, keep a list of those questions and look for their answers in the numbers, not on the slide.

There is one more thing a mentor must flag. Between October and November 2025 the Managing Director who had led most calls since 2023 resigned for personal reasons, seventeen days after chairing the Q2 FY26 call; Nilesh Koul, who comes from aluminium, replaced him. Aquapharm's CEO resigned in February 2026 and a successor arrived in May. Leadership change is not misconduct. It means the people who made the 2023 to 2025 promises are, in several cases, not the people who must keep them. That is also why I look to the CFO, Raj Gupta, who has been on every call since July 2022, as the continuity in this audit.

Let me give you my verdict on the dashboard in words you can hold on to. The carbon black engine works; it ramps new plants, earns above FY26 spreads and sells power at a good price. The acquisition and the balance sheet do not work yet; they are the reasons returns on capital are about 8%. I rate KPI health PASS_WITH_WATCH, at the weak end. I would move it to a fail if second-half spreads fall below about ₹16,500 a tonne without one-offs, or if Aquapharm stays below ₹45 crore a quarter and total debt stays above four times company EBITDA at March 2027. Next, in Chapter 6, we follow the cash and ask how much of all this reaches the shareholder.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Keep two ledgers when you listen to management. One records promises that depend on engineering, such as furnaces and co-generation, and PCBL keeps most of them, a little late. The other records promises that depend on markets, acquisitions and crude, and PCBL has missed most of them by large margins. An owner needs to price the second ledger, not the first.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A recovery you can see in one quarter is not a recovery you can count on. ₹22,900 and ₹19,800 a tonne in H1 FY27 each contained a one-off, and the underlying ₹17,900 is the number that has to hold when crude falls. Judge the next two quarters on that figure, on Aquapharm's ₹42 crore and on net debt, not on headline EBITDA.

book_callouts.title: KPI WATCHLIST FOR THE NEXT TWO QUARTERS
book_callouts.text: Five readings decide whether the PASS_WITH_WATCH rating improves or fails.
bullets: Carbon black EBITDA per tonne excluding inventory and refunds: at or above ₹17,000.
Quarterly volume: back above 150,000 t without discounting spot prices.
Aquapharm quarterly EBITDA: ₹60 crore or more, against ₹42 crore in Q2 FY27.
Net debt to company EBITDA: trending below 3.5x from 3.95x.
Andhra Pradesh environmental clearance and first nano-silicon customer qualification: dated, not promised.
